draft.title: Examples and counterexamples
card: A claim such as "every number of this type has this property" covers infinitely many cases. Checking a few cases is a test of the claim, not a proof of it.
a case where the claim works. Many examples can make a claim look likely, but they never prove it for all cases, because the next case might fail.
a single case where the claim fails. One is enough to disprove the claim, so it must be a case that fits the claim's conditions and gives a false result.

Worked example: "n² + n + 11 is prime for every whole number n ≥ 0." It works for n = 0, 1, 2 and more, giving 11, 13, 17. But n = 11 gives 121 + 11 + 11 = 143 = 11 × 13, which is not prime. So the claim is false.
draft.remember: Examples can support a claim, but one counterexample disproves it.

a.q: Priya says "n² + n + 11 is prime for every whole number n ≥ 0" because it works for n = 0 to 5. What do her six checks show?
opts: They support the claim but do not prove it
They prove the claim is true for all n
They prove the claim is false for some n
They show the claim is false after n = 5
a.why: Six successful checks are examples, and examples never cover every case. The claim is not proved, because a later case such as n = 11 could fail. It is also not disproved, because no failing case has been found.
a.clue: Did any of the six checks fail, and did they cover every n?

b.q: Claim: "If n is a whole number above 1, then n² − 1 is composite." Which value of n is a counterexample?
opts: n = 2, giving 3, which is prime
n = 5, giving 24, which is composite
n = 7, giving 48, which is composite
n = 1, giving 0, which is not composite
b.why: For n = 2, n² − 1 = 3, which is prime, so the claim fails for a case that fits its conditions. The values n = 5 and n = 7 are examples that agree with the claim. n = 1 is not above 1, so it does not fit the claim's conditions and cannot be a counterexample.
b.clue: A counterexample must meet the condition and make the result false.

a.best: They support the claim but do not prove it

check.summary: No problems found. The facts check out: n² + n + 11 is prime for n = 0 to 5 and gives 143 = 11 × 13 at n = 11, and n = 2 is the only counterexample because n² − 1 = (n − 1)(n + 1) is composite for every n > 2.
